title: Fermilab, IBM And NVIDIA Plan Quantum Computing Co-design Platform
excerpt: Fermilab, IBM plan modular quantum computing co-design platform to advance scientific discovery.
content:
Fermilab, IBM and NVIDIA announced a collaboration on November 16, 2026, to build a co-design platform for modular quantum computing focused on the demanding needs of high-energy and nuclear physics. The initiative expands upon existing work at Fermilab’s Superconducting Quantum Materials and Systems (SQMS) Center, uniting quantum hardware with accelerated computing to tackle problems including particle interactions and neutrino physics.

“This intended platform presents an extraordinary opportunity,” said Anna Grassellino, Fermilab chief technology officer and director of the SQMS Center. The platform aims to co-design applications and architectures needed for fault-tolerant quantum computing useful for scientific discovery.

SQMS Center Drives Modular Quantum System Co-Design

Fermilab, IBM, and NVIDIA are focusing their collaborative efforts on specific scientific challenges. Particle interactions, neutrino physics, and nuclear simulations will be initial targets for the new co-design platform. This focused approach distinguishes the project from broader quantum computing initiatives and demonstrates a clear intent to apply quantum resources to pressing problems in high-energy and nuclear physics.

The SQMS Center’s existing infrastructure and expertise in superconducting technologies provide a solid foundation for this expansion, accelerating the development of specialized quantum algorithms and hardware. The partnership intends to unite advanced quantum processors with accelerated computing platforms, a strategy designed to overcome limitations in both technologies.

NVIDIA’s contributions will center on its accelerated computing capabilities, aiming to enhance the classical processing needed to support and interpret quantum computations. “With Fermilab and NVIDIA, we’re exploring how these real-world problems can help us shape the modular, interconnected architectures that will define the next generation of quantum computers and accelerated classical computing,” a representative stated, highlighting the synergistic nature of the collaboration.

The collaboration envisions a future where quantum processors function as powerful instruments for scientific discovery, smoothly integrated into existing workflows. “Fermilab, IBM and NVIDIA are showing how quantum can be brought into the heart of scientific research with hybrid quantum-classical systems,” according to the announcement, signaling a shift towards practical quantum applications.

The SQMS Center, already a collaboration of over 40 institutions, will use Fermilab’s experience in building complex particle accelerators to engineer multiqubit quantum processor platforms. “Some of the most fundamental problems in science remain out of reach for classical computers alone. Scaling quantum and classical systems together will open new frontiers in high-energy and nuclear physics and beyond,” they added, emphasizing the potential for transformative breakthroughs. Integrating quantum computing with superconducting workflows, they believe, will dramatically expand the scope of scientific inquiry.

IBM, NVIDIA and Fermilab Integrate Quantum-Classical Architectures

Fermilab intends to integrate its ultracoherent superconducting cavity hardware into the co-design platform following initial work with IBM, a step that expands the scope of existing quantum hardware collaboration at the SQMS Center. Researchers will investigate these cavities not only as quantum memories but also as entanglement buffers and resources for bosonic error correction, exploring alternative pathways to stabilize quantum information. This focus on physical interconnects and cavities distinguishes the effort from purely software-based approaches to quantum computing, prioritizing hardware co-design for specific scientific challenges.

Contributions center on decoding, simulation, optimization and real-time feedback mechanisms, important for managing the complex data streams generated by quantum processors. This division reflects a strategy to address the limitations of both quantum and classical computing, using each technology’s strengths to overcome the other’s weaknesses. The collaboration extends beyond a single laboratory, aiming to facilitate knowledge exchange between DOE’s National Quantum Information Science Research Centers. Teams will share software, benchmarking methods and lessons learned to accelerate the development of future user facilities.

HENP Applications Guide Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing Development

This expansion moves beyond foundational research, aiming to directly address the challenges of connecting quantum hardware with real-world scientific problems. The initiative seeks to establish a physical co-location of IBM quantum computers and NVIDIA accelerated computing resources at Fermilab, creating an integrated environment for quantum processing and data analysis. The platform’s design prioritizes the needs of high-energy and nuclear physicists, with a specific focus on co-designing applications and algorithms tailored for fault-tolerant quantum computing.

Fermilab will contribute expertise in superconducting cavity research and interconnects, essential for scaling quantum systems, alongside its established role in supporting large scientific collaborations. “Our ambition is to help lead the development of quantum computers built for discovery,” said a representative from Fermilab, emphasizing the goal of creating a system useful for scientific advancement.

This approach differs from the recently launched co-design platform involving IBM, Oak Ridge National Laboratory and AMD, which concentrates on quantum error correction and materials science. The long-term vision extends beyond a single facility, aiming to cultivate a robust scientific user community and establish the necessary technology and software infrastructure for future scalable quantum computing facilities.

This collaborative effort will integrate quantum processors into existing scientific workflows and address the practical challenges of operating complex quantum systems. The partners intend to connect quantum hardware design with the needs of scientific users from the outset, ensuring that the technology is developed with specific applications in mind and that the resulting systems are optimized for tackling complex scientific problems.
